overview: This week's papers share a concern with how robust a claimed mechanism or difference really is. A stress test of a connectome-constrained fly vision model [found that circuit-level conclusions shift](#p7) with the attribution method, the circuit representation, and the trained solution, and that some behavioral signatures also appear in matched CNNs. A similar caution runs through [work on language models answering psychological scales](#p5), where a cross-language difference in trait was offset by a difference in response bias on scales without reverse-keyed items. A [large sentence-picture experiment on scalar implicature](#p4) likewise found that the predicted polarity effect varied across scales and was only weakly supported. On the more positive side, [six preregistered studies of a Battleship-style game](#p3) found that players randomized close to optimally in a competitive setting, which suggests that earlier claims about human randomization limits may depend on the tasks used. A [framework that varies retrieval competition in Hopfield-like networks](#p0) showed the same stored traces yielding different kinds of generalization, an argument for one flexible hippocampus-like system over separate memory systems. Among the developmental and clinical findings, [pre-reading toddlers from English, Spanish and Hebrew communities](#p2) showed naming directions that matched their culture's writing direction, and [EEG entrainment to non-speech rhythms](#p6) predicted dyslexia well, pointing to a phonemic entrainment deficit.

papers.title: The Same Memory Retrieved Differently: Competition Enables Flexible Generalization in Hippocampus-like Networks
papers.summary: Instead of positing separate memory systems for specific and general knowledge, the researchers present ATHENA, a framework that treats cognitive memory models as recurrent networks, similar to Modern Hopfield Networks. The key knob is how intense the competition is during retrieval: in simulations, changing it makes the same stored traces yield different kinds of generalization. They also extend the idea to sequential memory, which makes a case that one hippocampus-like system can be both detailed and flexible.
papers.abstract: Hippocampus supports the retrieval of richly detailed episodic memories from sparse cues. However, an event can be detailed and also lead to generalization. To explain both phenomena, researchers have proposed multiple memory systems or distinct memory traces for specific and general content. In contrast, we argue that a single system can support both specificity and generalization. To do this, we present ATHENA, a formal framework that reinterprets cognitive memory models as recurrent neural networks. We show that many episodic memory models are single-step approximations of dynamic networks with competitive retrieval mechanisms, similar to Modern Hopfield Networks. Notably, under a cognitive interpretation, the intensity of the competitive process is a psychologically-meaningful parameter that shapes generalization in the network. Through simulations, we demonstrate that modulating this parameter during retrieval leads the same traces to produce qualitatively different forms of generalization over the same memory traces. We then extend our analysis to sequential memory, and show how the same competitive retrieval process can be combined with known hippocampal circuits to achieve more sophisticated forms of generalization. These results demonstrate the flexibility of single-system memory retrieval and highlight the interplay of specific and general mnemonic content.

papers.title: Interpretability in the Limit: How Can Understanding Machines Help us Understand Human Language?
papers.summary: Suppose interpretability research succeeds beyond our hopes and maps out the internal mechanisms of LLMs. What should linguists and cognitive scientists do with them? The paper offers ways to classify these machine constructs (by theoretical, domain and ontological status, and by complexity) and argues for focusing on ones that recur across very different models. It also says these constructs should be treated as hypotheses for domain experts to test, not as answers, and ends with recommendations that could be put to use now.
papers.abstract: In the coming years, interpretability research will uncover a vast set of machine constructs: causally efficacious representations and processing mechanisms underlying the use of language and other intelligent behavior in AI systems, including LLMs. Assuming that interpretability will be as successful as can be reasonably hoped for (interpretability in the limit), how can the discovery of machine constructs shape linguistics and cognitive science? First, we provide several axes of analysis that can help scientists conceptualize the internal mechanisms discovered in machines. Even under the assumption that interpretability in the limit guarantees that all constructs are causally implicated in a system's behavior, scientists may want to consider several additional properties, including constructs' theoretical status, domain status, ontological status, and complexity. Second, we argue that scientists should prioritize recurrent constructs, meaning those that surface across a diversity of models converging on behaviors of interest while varying on other axes such as architecture, training data, objective function, language, and modality. Finally, we provide three routes for how machine constructs can inform linguistic and cognitive theories, emphasizing that all of these routes treat machine constructs as hypotheses, where additional theorizing and experimentation by domain experts are required. We conclude with several recommendations that can be implemented now for improving the long-term success of this program.

papers.title: The emergence of language-specific biases in visual attention in pre-reading toddlers from two cultures
papers.summary: Toddlers aged 2.5 to 4, from English, Spanish and Hebrew-speaking communities, named pictured objects in a picture naming task. Hebrew learners tended to name objects right-to-left, while English and Spanish learners went the other way, and the pattern grew stronger with age. Since these kids can't read yet, the work suggests that attention is shaped by the direction of a culture's writing before any literacy instruction.
papers.abstract: Skilled adult readers show biases in their visual attention that reflect the direction of their native writing systems (e.g., English readers scan left-to-right while Hebrew readers scan right-to-left), but it not yet clear when these biases develop. We tested the hypothesis that language-specific patterns of behavior precede the ability to read by testing how toddlers (2.5-4 years) exposed to different writing systems allocated their attention in a picture naming task. Across two communities, children tended to name objects in the direction that matched their native language. Hebrew-learning toddlers labeled objects from right-to-left, while English- and Spanish-learning toddlers showed the reverse pattern, and language-specific tendencies strengthened with age. These results demonstrate that children have begun to discover directional regularities associated with their language even before they receive literacy instruction and illustrate how cultural conventions exert a direct influence on children’s attention from a very young age.

papers.title: Near-random behavior in strategic games
papers.authors: Tal Boger, Dorsa Amir, Sami R. Yousif
papers.summary: People are famously bad at acting randomly when asked to, but this team asked whether a competitive setting changes that. Using an online Battleship-style game on a 3×3 grid, across six preregistered studies, they found that players behaved close to optimally random, much more so than in matched non-strategic tasks. Players also adjusted sensibly when tiles differed in value and when they considered what their opponent knew. A computational model backed this up, so the old conclusion that humans can't randomize may reflect the tasks used.
papers.abstract: Humans struggle to produce random behavior when asked to do so, leading some to suggest that our ability to randomize is attenuated (or even absent). Here, we demonstrate that the capacity for random behavior is much greater than previously acknowledged: Humans can behave in (near) optimally random ways when the context demands it. We created a custom, online version of the game Battleship in which participants competed against one another. On each turn, one player chose a tile on a 3 × 3 grid to place a ship, while the other player tried to guess the ship's location. Across six preregistered studies, this strategic context led to dramatic increases in random behavior relative to closely matched non-strategic tasks. Such random behavior was also remarkably flexible and optimal depending on context; both players readily incorporated varying information about the game (e.g., that tiles can differ in value) while simultaneously accounting for their opponents' knowledge of that information. A computational model validated these findings and revealed nuanced differences across contexts. Contrary to decades of work finding that humans fail to randomize, we find that strategic games promote highly flexible, near-random behavior.

papers.title: Polarity and the speed of scalar implicature processing
papers.summary: A hypothesis in pragmatics predicts that scalar implicatures like 'some' meaning 'some but not all' should be slower to process than literal readings, while the reverse should hold for negative terms like 'not all'. In a sentence-picture verification experiment with 538 participants, the researchers found no clear support for this, and the effect varied a lot across scales. A meta-analysis with earlier work gave a small effect in the predicted direction, and even the classic general slowdown for implicatures appeared only in early trials. Polarity may matter, but not robustly across scales.
papers.abstract: Scalar implicatures (SIs) such as the inference from 'some' to 'some but not all' are known to vary in processing cost. According to the Polarity Hypothesis (van Tiel et al., 2019; van Tiel & Pankratz, 2021), this cost depends on the polarity of the scalar term: SIs from positively polar expressions (e.g., 'some' implicating 'some but not all') are expected to be slower to compute than literal interpretations, while the reverse should hold for SIs from negatively polar expressions, sometimes referred to as indirect SIs (e.g., 'not all' implicating 'not all but some'). We tested this prediction in a sentence–picture verification experiment with 538 English-speaking participants. Each participant judged whether sentences containing weak or strong scalar terms matched a corresponding picture, allowing us to measure response times as an index of processing effort. Our results showed no clear evidence for the Polarity Hypothesis effect. Specifically, we found that the effect strongly varies across the different scales included in our experiment. We additionally conducted a meta-analysis pooling our estimate with all existing evidence so far: the pooled effect is small and in the predicted direction, but the study-specific estimates behind it vary widely in magnitude. Surprisingly, our results do also not clearly validate the traditional assumption of a B&N effect (Bott & Noveck, 2004), i.e., a general polarity-independent processing slowdown under SIs: a subsequent analysis including trial order revealed that the B&N effect was present in early trials of our study, whereas later trials do not show the effect. Overall, we conclude that polarity may influence the speed of scalar implicature processing, but that this effect is not robust across all types of scales.

papers.title: Trait or Bias? Why item keying is indispensable when comparing language model responses across languages
papers.summary: When language models answer psychological scales differently in Chinese and English, people often read that as a cultural difference. Here, four US and Chinese models took three social orientation scales in both languages, and a psychometric model split the responses into a latent trait and a directional response bias. On balanced scales, Chinese prompting gave a higher trait and lower bias, and the two offset each other on scales without reverse-keyed items, so a reported difference there can't be taken as a difference in the construct. The authors propose three checks for cross-linguistic comparisons: balanced keying, item-level decomposition, and contemporaneous controls.
papers.abstract: Psychological scales designed for humans are increasingly administered to language models, and differences between their responses in two languages are read as evidence of cultural tendency. Such comparisons presuppose that the two language versions measure the same thing. This study tests that premise. Three established social orientation scales were administered to four models built by United States and Chinese developers in Chinese and English under two temperature settings. Responses were then decomposed, using a psychometric model that separates a latent trait from a directional response bias, into the component that tracks what the instrument is meant to measure and the component that does not. The cross-linguistic difference is not one quantity. On scales with balanced keying, every estimate showed a higher trait and a lower bias under Chinese prompting, the bias moving further than the trait in most conditions. Because the two components run in opposite directions, they offset one another on scales containing no reverse-keyed items, where they also cannot be separated. A difference reported on such a scale therefore does not establish that models differ in the construct, only that they answered differently. Two further manipulations show that the difference is produced by item wording, though not by negation, and that the stability of a model identifier over four weeks varies by an order of magnitude between vendors. We set out three checks that would make cross-linguistic comparison interpretable: balanced keying, decomposition to the item level, and a contemporaneous control whenever collections are compared across time.

papers.title: EEG Entrainment to Non-Speech Rhythmic Patterns Associated with Dimensions of Language Performance
papers.authors: Francisco J. Martínez-Murcia, Nicolás J. Gallego-Molina, Marco A. Formoso et al.
papers.summary: Looking at 48 participants, the researchers recorded EEG while people listened to white noise whose amplitude was modulated at rates matching Spanish speech units, and asked whether brain entrainment to those non-speech rhythms could identify dyslexia. Phase-amplitude coupling at the 40 Hz stimulus predicted dyslexia well (balanced accuracy 0.929 in the best case), pointing to a phonemic entrainment deficit. Among controls, poorer phonemic awareness, reading comprehension, or rapid naming went with stronger right-hemisphere entrainment, which fits the idea of hemispheric compensation.
papers.abstract: Developmental dyslexia (DLX) affects 5-12% of the global population and impairs learning to read. Its biological basis, particularly the difficulties observed in oral phonological tasks, remains debated. Entrainment, the coupling of brain oscillations to speech rhythms, is essential for encoding phonological representations. We investigated whether brain entrainment to non-speech rhythms could predict DLX in 48 participants listening to white noise amplitude-modulated at rates matching Spanish speech units. Phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) analysis of electroencephalography (EEG) signals yielded accurate DLX prediction for the 40 Hz stimulus using the Heights Ratio PAC measure (balanced accuracy 0.929, p = 0.0069, in the best case), indicating a stronger phonemic entrainment deficit in dyslexic individuals. Regression analysis in control (CTL) participants showed a strong dependence between reading performance scores and greater entrainment in language-associated brain regions. In particular, participants with poorer phonemic awareness, reading comprehension, or rapid automatized naming showed greater right-hemisphere entrainment to the 40 Hz stimulus. This finding adds evidence for the hemispheric compensatory mechanisms hypothesized in the literature. In conclusion, our methodology identifies dyslexia-specific entrainment patterns near language-associated brain regions, together with compensatory entrainment in right-hemisphere areas.

papers.title: FlyHack: Stress-Testing Mechanistic Claims in a Connectome-Constrained Visual Model
papers.summary: Connectome-constrained models promise that we can test circuit mechanisms directly, but this paper checks how fragile those conclusions are, using the flyvis fly motion-vision model along with task-matched CNN controls. Some behavioral signatures, like reverse-phi reversal, also show up in the CNNs, and the adversarial robustness gap over CNNs largely closes for larger ones. Circuit-level conclusions also depend on the attribution method, on how the circuit is represented, and on which of the 50 trained models you look at. The takeaway is that these models make hypotheses testable, but claims should be scoped to the specific model family, intervention, and trained solution.
papers.abstract: Connectome-constrained neural networks make biological components directly accessible to intervention, but their mechanistic conclusions can still depend on the comparison model, intervention, circuit representation and trained solution. We stress-test these dependencies in flyvis, a \emph{Drosophila} motion-vision model, using its 50-model ensemble, task-matched causal CNN controls and replicated interventions. At the level of model behaviour, three-level reverse-phi reversal in flyvis is strongly period- and velocity-dependent and also appears in task-matched CNNs; neither family reproduces the fly's stationary-sawtooth response. Adversarial direction reversal requires a perturbation bound of 0.21--0.27 times stimulus contrast in flyvis versus 0.13--0.25 in CNNs, but the gap over a parameter-matched CNN largely closes for larger CNNs. At the level of mechanism, matching attribution to the intervention matters: for held-out-mean replacement, first-order edge attribution patching reaches pooled AUROC 0.970 and Spearman 0.872, versus 0.933 and 0.126 when its zero-aligned score is evaluated against the same ground truth. Circuit conclusions also vary with representation and ensemble member. Greedy cell-type sets meet a model-relative T4/T5 tuning criterion in 25 of 50 models, while T4/T5 output silencing reduces the tested optic-flow behaviour to at most two of eight clips in 40. In six models where the cell-type search first succeeds, the corresponding connection sets can be pruned to 13--31 added classes; under an additional two-sided response-amplitude check, only two of those six first-success cell-type sets still meet the tuning threshold. These results support a narrower use of connectome-constrained models: they make mechanistic hypotheses directly testable, but the resulting claims must be scoped to the model family, intervention, representation and trained solution.

papers.title: Examining the Relations Between Self-Construal, Culture, and Cognitive Dissonance Using the Induced Compliance Paradigm
papers.summary: Does cognitive dissonance work differently depending on culture and on how people see themselves in relation to others? Using a large international dataset (18 countries, N = 3,804) in a registered report, the researchers looked at the induced-compliance paradigm, which avoids the validity worries around the free-choice paradigm used in earlier cross-cultural work. Neither individual self-construal, national individualism, nor country-level self-construal moderated dissonance effects as predicted. That suggests earlier cultural differences may not carry over to this paradigm, and the authors call for revisiting the procedure's reliability and the role of choice.
papers.abstract: Cognitive dissonance, traditionally conceptualized as a fundamental psychological process involving discomfort from inconsistent cognitions, may vary across cultures. These variations could be attributed to self-construal, or how individuals define themselves in relation to others. Although previous cross-cultural research has predominantly used the free-choice paradigm, significant concerns have been raised regarding its procedural validity and the robustness of its findings. To address this issue, this registered report presents secondary analyses of a large-scale international dataset. We investigated the moderating role of cultural variables on dissonance effects within the induced-compliance paradigm across 18 countries (N = 3,804). We hypothesized that dissonance effects would be stronger for participants with higher individual-level self-construal scores (H1), in more individualistic countries (H2), and in countries with higher country-level self-construal scores (H3). Our results did not support these hypotheses, suggesting that cultural moderation may not generalize to the induced-compliance paradigm. We discuss the necessity of reassessing the procedure’s reliability and clarifying the theoretical role of choice.

papers.title: Ulyssean Self-Control: Pre-commitment is effective, but choosing it freely requires good self-control
papers.summary: Pre-commitment can help with self-control, but the people who most need it may be the least likely to use it. In Study 1 (N = 1,012), pre-commitment improved effort performance in an incentivized task. In Study 2 (N = 1,010), people low in trait self-control were 35 percentage points less likely to choose it, and did worse as a result; telling people it works nudged uptake up slightly, while forced pre-commitment did best. Study 3 (N = 1,037) found the same pattern across work, education, and health, mediated by future focus, strategy familiarity, and temptation avoidance.
papers.abstract: Can pre-commitment strategies be a solution to self-control problems, or do they mainly help those who are already successful at regulating their behavior? In Study 1 (N=1,012), pre-commitment causally improved effort performance in an incentivized matrix-solving task. However, in Study 2 (N=1,010) participants with low (vs. high) self-control as a general trait were 35 percentage points less likely to choose the pre-commitment strategy, which in turn was associated with worse performance and earnings. Information about strategy effectiveness led to a small increase in uptake, whereas a “paternalistic” policy with forced pre-commitment led to superior performance. Study 3 (N=1,037) found that participants with high trait self-control were more likely to choose pre-commitment strategies across work, education, and health domains, mediated by higher future focus, strategy familiarity, and temptation avoidance. Pre-commitment is an effective strategy, but it is most often chosen by those who are already doing well: Individuals with good self-control.

papers.title: Aging and Hearing Loss in Emotional Prosody Processing: Divergent Neural Adaptation and Behavioral Performance
papers.summary: Two experiments combined ERPs, time-frequency analyses and behavior to separate the roles of aging and hearing loss in processing emotion in speech. Older adults showed weaker neural differentiation between emotions, slower and less efficient behavior, and larger P3a responses, while hearing sensitivity had no main effect on accuracy or reaction time despite delayed early neural responses and stronger theta and alpha activity. Because neural and behavioral results didn't always line up, the authors propose an 'asymmetric adaptation' account in which the brain reorganizes selectively across processing stages in response to degraded input.
papers.abstract: Emotional prosody perception is vulnerable in later adulthood, yet the contributions of central aging and peripheral hearing loss remain unclear. Across two experiments, we combined event-related potentials (ERPs) , time-frequency analyses and behavioral measures to examine how aging and hearing sensitvity shape emotional prosody processing. Experiment 1 used acoustically matched speech and nonspeech stimuli in a passive oddball paradigm to assess preattentive processing. Experiment 2 examined explicit emotion identification and implicit stimulus judgment to evaluate goal-directed performance and its associations with neural responses. Aging was associated with reduced neural differentiation between emotions and lower behavioral efficiency, alongside enhanced P3a amplitude. Older adults also responded more slowly than younger adults during emotion identification. Hearing sensitivity showed no significant main effect on accuracy or reaction time, despite associations with delayed early neural processing and stronger theta- and alpha-band activity. Hearing-related neural effects were most evident in older adults and varied across emotions and stimulus types. Brain–behavior associations were selective: reduced mismatch negativity (MMN) was associated with slower responses during stimulus identification, whereas longer MMN latencies were associated with lower accuracy and slower responses during emotion identification. These findings indicate that aging and hearing loss have distinct yet interacting associations with emotional prosody processing, with neural responses not necessarily corresponding to behavioral performance. We propose an “asymmetric adaptation” account in which neural responses to degraded auditory input reorganize selectively across processing stages and contexts, potentially explaining this neural-behavioral divergence and informing more sensitive assessment of socioemotional communication in later adulthood.

papers.title: Effects of a Web-Based Debiasing Intervention on Brazilian Psychologists’ Accuracy on Major Depressive Disorder Diagnostic Tasks: A Randomized Training Intervention
papers.summary: A brief web-based training that teaches Bayesian probability estimates and other debiasing strategies was adapted from earlier work on pediatric bipolar disorder and tried out on Brazilian psychologists (N = 535, 299 assessed afterward) judging depression vignettes. Those who got it made fewer decision-making errors and diagnosed more accurately than an active control group, especially on the risk-estimation vignette, though not on purely categorical diagnostic tasks. The effects were much smaller than in the original intervention, so this is preliminary evidence that the training transfers across clinical and cultural settings.
papers.abstract: This randomized experimental study evaluated a web-based debiasing intervention designed to improve clinical judgment in the assessment of adult major depressive disorder (MDD) in Brazil. The intervention, adapted from prior work on pediatric bipolar disorder, taught Bayesian probability estimates and other debiasing strategies. Brazilian psychologists (N = 535) were assigned to either the intervention or an active control condition featuring a brief educational video, and were assessed post-intervention (n = 299). Outcomes were decision-making errors and diagnostic accuracy in response to vignettes, which depicted diagnostic challenges that could elicit cognitive biases. Assignment to intervention was associated with significantly fewer decision-making errors and greater diagnostic accuracy. Intervention effects were stronger for the vignette involving diagnostic risk estimation, as supported by intervention-by-vignette interaction effects. Intervention effects across vignettes were not statistically significant when only categorical diagnostic tasks were considered. Years of clinical practice and postgraduate training were largely unrelated to outcomes, and decision-making errors were not associated with treatment decisions. Overall, findings provide preliminary evidence of the transferability of this brief, web-based debiasing intervention to a distinct clinical and cultural context, although effect sizes were substantially attenuated compared with those observed in the original intervention.

papers.title: PRELIMINARY FRAMEWORK FOR A DYNAMIC SOCIO-ACOUSTIC MODEL OF SPEECH PERCEPTION
papers.summary: Here's a conceptual proposal, not an experiment: a Dynamic Socio-Acoustic Model in which speech perception is continuous, multidimensional tracking of acoustic detail. Listeners keep an exemplar space not tied to linguistic units and build categories on the fly, stretching and rescaling their perceptual space in response to the contrasts in the immediate context. The upshot is that variation in speech is treated as a route to social meaning instead of noise to overcome.
papers.abstract: Listeners store detailed acoustic information and access social information cued by variation fast and early. Yet, how we understand all we understand remains an open question. I propose a Dynamic Socio-Acoustic Model that frames perception as a continuous, multidimensional tracking system where speech variation functions as primary cognitive information. This listener-driven model includes the fluid topological stretching of cognitive space, an acoustic exemplar space that is untethered to linguistic units and allows for multidimensional cross-context categorization. Listeners maintain a sub-lexical, macro-exemplar landscape where incoming acoustic-kinematic trajectories drive real-time resonance. Rather than matching signals to static templates, listeners construct ad-hoc categories on the fly, dynamically scaling an active grid in response to immediate environmental contrasts. By uniting continuous sensory tracking with fluid, experience-dependent spatial restructuring, this framework offers an ecological account of perception and memory that rethinks structural variation from a hurdle into a pathway to social meaning.
